body: @bdoubrov @DuffJohnson @mrbhardy - please weigh in. Happy if you wish to take discussion to another TWG first...

I would say that `null` is allowed only in **StructTreeRoot/ParentTree** and not permitted in all other places listed above. 

To me the presence of `null` in  **StructTreeRoot/ParentTree** should be an implication of a more general statement that `null` is permitted as a value in both `name-tree` and `number-tree` data structures with the same provision as `null` values in dictionaries:
> A dictionary entry whose value is `null` (see 7.3.9, "Null object") shall be treated the same as if the entry does not exist.

Re: StructTreeRoot/ParentTree . . .
- can an element in that array be null? 

This would presumably indicate that there is a MCS content item that has no parent element (whose reference must be at that index in the array)!  

Such orphaned content items (with an MCID) seem unlikely to actually exist, so what meaning does this "popular implementation" give to such use of 'null'? :   It would appear at least one popular implementation uses 'null`.

Re StructTreeRoot/K :

Table 354 clearly states that this either a single dictionary or an array of dictionaries.  

But the null object is definitely not a dictionary, so how can this value be legal here?

> ... or an array of dictionaries.

So where an element _in_ the array is `null`: `[ ... null ... ]` - not a null array. 

So consider these situations:
* `/K [ ]`
* `/K [ null ]`
* `/K [ 10 0 R null 11 0 R ]`

Which ones do you think are valid?

**StructTreeRoot/ParentTree** is more awkward to do as an example as it is a number tree. From Table 354 "_the value shall be an array of references to the parent elements of those marked-content sequences_" - can this array have `null` array elements? `[ 10 0 R null 11 0 R ]` where `10 0 R` and `11 0 R` are valid parents?

Using `null` as a value in the **StructTreeRoot/ParentTree** (or in any `name-tree` or `number-tree`) is a very pragmatic solution for deleting elements from the tree. The only alternative would be rebuilding the tree, which is often too ineffective and, in case of **StructTreeRoot/ParentTree**, might require modifying MCID properties of marked content sequences in the content stream.

> Using `null` as a value in the **StructTreeRoot/ParentTree** ...

I'm referring to the _value_ of the name-/number-tree that is an _array_ and that array then having `null` elements. 
So **not** the value elements of the **Nums** or **Names** arrays, although what you say is also relevant.

But I would be nervous about making global assumptions that every name-tree or number-tree in PDF can always accept `null` as an acceptable value without first explicitly checking wording of each use. In the same way that assuming an empty array `[ ]` or array with only nulls `[ null ]` are the same - as we need to check for any requirements about array lengths, etc.

You are right, I meant `null` elements inside arrays forming values in **StructTreeRoot/ParentTree**. Like this example taken from a real world document:
```
<<
/Type /StructTreeRoot
...
/ParentTree
    <<
     /Nums [0 [23 0 R null null 24 0 R 24 0 R] 2 [18 0 R 19 0 R 20 0 R 21 0 R] ]     
    >> 
>>
```
I agree this is different from having `null` as an element in the array value of **Nums** in the `number-tree`. So, I'm no longer sure why a creator of this particular example does not remove `null` values and sometimes (as in the example above) duplicates elements in the arrays in the **ParentTree**.

Yes indeed, so what can the null values possibly mean here? :

[23 0 R null null 24 0 R 24 0 R]

But note that it is not possible to remove values from these arrays as they are indexed by the fixed MCIDs of actual content items.

But since each such content item has a parent structure, the use of null here must surely be an error.

In this particular example the use case was to merge two structure elements into one. So, in the structure tree two elements were deleted and one added. The two `null`s in the parent tree correspond to the deleted structure elements and the duplicated  one (`24 0 R`) corresponds to the new merged structure element.

It seems that is just wrong.  These entries are not indexed by structure elements but by content items with MCIDs.

Merging a structure element does not remove its content items from the stream, they are still there and have MCIDs.  The structure element that is now the parent will need to be changed, but surely every content item with an MCID will still have a parent structure item. 

If content items with MCIDs can exist that do not have any parent structure item, then how to represent this case should be explicitly documented in 14.7.5.4.

Currently it states only this:
 
"For a content stream containing marked-content sequences that are content items, the value shall be an array of indirect references to the sequences’ parent structure elements. 
The array element corresponding to each sequence shall be found by using the sequence’s marked-content identifier as a zero-based index into the array."

I just ran a test over about 100,000 PDFs and a LOT of PDFs have this idiom with `null` in the array form of **StructTreeRoot/ParentTree** number-tree values (some with 100s and 1000s of instances)! But none of the other logical structure-related dict entries listed in my original post had `null` entries.

I did **not** check the content streams and whether any MCID still indexed those `null` array elements.

I think I can see one (more?) good reason for there being many nulls in these arrays. 

This cause highlights a more general failing with the documentation of how these arrays, indexed by MCIDs, should work. 

Some explanation of how these nulls arise: 

The MCID numbers of the content items in a content stream can be arbitrary integers, they need not form a 'complete integer interval' such as {0,1,2,3,4,5}; they can be any set, such as {0,2,4}, or even (in theory) {0,2,4,652}.

But such a set of MCID numbers themselves must be used as indices into these arrays, thus in the second example above, the array would need to be of length 5, and in the final example 653.  This is somewhat strange but it is the reality to be dealt with.  But it is not covered in 14.7.5.4 or, I believe, anywhere else.

Sets of MCIDs such as {0,2,4} arise vey naturally and there is no prescription for what entry to use in the "missing indices",  1 and 3 in this case.  Thus "null" is used as a pragmatic solution that seems to work.  

This pragmatic solution needs to be documented (as does the one below). 

The following, distinct, possibility was previously indicated by @bdoubrov: 

When an existing MCID number is that of a content item that has no structural parent.  It is not clear whether this should also be indicated by using a null in this array; it maybe needs a different value, such as using the root node of the structure tree.

There is an existing discussion in subclause 14.7.5.4 "Finding structure elements from content items" regarding MCIDs and the **ParentTree**, but it does not cover the cases we're discussing here. Interestingly searching for MCID does not find subclause 14.7.5.4 so this info is difficult to find... 

Trying to summarize:
* as far as my original post goes, we've settled that _ONLY_ **StructTreeRoot/ParentTree** in its array form can validly have array elements that are `null`. 
* subclause 14.7.5.4 "Finding structure elements from content items" needs to state that `null` array entries can be used for unused marked-content identifiers - e.g. in the 2nd bullet above the NOTE and Table 354. This is a "can"/"may", not a "shall". This is @car222222's point above. 
*  subclause 14.7.5.4 "Finding structure elements from content items" needs to state that `null` array entries shall be used for marked-content identifiers that do not have any structural parent  - e.g. in the 2nd bullet above the NOTE. This is @bdoubrov's point.
* all the other entries I mentioned in the original post **shall not** have array elements that are `null` - these file format requirements need to be added to the description of each of those entries in Table 354 or 355.
* subclause 14.7.5.4 "Finding structure elements from content items" needs an editorial change so that the acronym "MCID" is mentioned as this is what most people search for. e.g. as a parenthetical in the 2nd bullet above the NOTE.

These are all file format requirements, not processor requirements.

Did I miss anything?
@bdoubrov @mrbhardy - can you please confirm the above prior to our next PDF TWG

I have not checked all the details here 
(apologies) but I can see no obvious deficiencies.

Here is one extra possible refinement to consider, re:

"* subclause 14.7.5.4 "Finding structure elements from content items" needs to state that null array entries shall be used for marked-content identifiers that do not have any structural parent"

It might be better to recommend using something other than a "null" value for such an MCID index in the array, so as to clearly distinguish this case, when the index is the MCID of a content item, from the case of a "non-existent" MCID (the previous bullet point).

One possibility is to use for this case the structure tree root.

This makes some sense since, even if there are no surviving structure ﻿elements in the tree, the structure tree root must survive in order for the "parents" number tree to be defined, without which these arrays cannot not even be accessed. 
If there is no structure tree root, then there is no "parents tree" and then there are no arrays indexed by MCIDs.  

A useful result of this change will be a better outcome from the following events: 
a content item in a content stream starts off with an MCID and a normal structure tree parent, but then subsequently the structure tree gets pruned in such a way that the content item gets totally orphaned (i.e., it has no structure parent).
If this happens then it is natural to make the structure tree root become the new parent of the content item.

> One possibility is to use for this case the structure tree root.

That would imho not be allowed. If a MC points to a structure element as its parent, this structure element should also contain this MC as a kid, but the root can't contain content items as kid.

A good point.

So, is there a better way to make this important distinction between existing and non-existent MCIDs?

Although, of course, the "structure tree root" is not in fact a "structure element", so this stricture (that it must have the MC item as a kid) does not apply to it. 

The idea is that this is simply better than using "null" as the "distinguished value" for both cases.  Like "null" it is really just a name, not an actual "structure parent".

> Although, of course, the "structure tree root" is not in fact a "structure element"

StructTreeRoot is explicitly mentioned in the matrix with a list of allowed children, and content items are not one of them:

![image](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/assets/4047173/8267076c-49fe-4b14-bcf3-1d9b5153fab1)

But even if that were allowed: How would you then distinguish between "wanted" MCID put there by purpose and "unwanted" MCID which only got pushed out of other structures, e.g. because they are empty and should be ignored? Actually the main use of the null entry for us, is to hide empty MCID the code produces and it would be a bit contra productive to make them visible again by moving them into the root.

But no one is adding any children to the root, it is merely used as an arbitrary marker, that is not "null".  

If no one likes it then choose something else, such as "the integer 0".

I'd never noticed that "StructTreeRoot" in Table Annex L.2 - thanks for pointing that out!

It's also not correct as to how the table captions itself, as **StructTreeRoot** is not a "... _standard structure elements in the standard structure namespace_ ...". It's a dictionary. But it also clearly says there is a "precisely 1" relationship - there is **_no_** zero so it always needs to be present.

I think this should be removed and phrased in English, something like the following - possibly in/around Table 364: 
> For the structure element dictionary (Table 355) that has a structure type of **Document**, the value of the **P** entry in that structure element dictionary shall be an indirect reference to the structure tree root dictionary (Table 354). There shall always be exactly one such structure element dictionary for PDF files containing structure hierarchy.

I had also just now discovered the strangeness that StructTreeRoot (suddenly) appears as a Structure Type in Table L.2! 

But sorting that out probably needs a separate, new issue.

I would like to endorse @car222222's proposal about the **distinction between parent tree array elements for ~deleted~/nonexistent/unused and orphaned content items** (my considerations are in the second half of this comment, here below):

@car222222 [(see comment 1717316365)](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/308#issuecomment-1717316365):
> It might be better to recommend using something other than a "null" value for such an MCID index in the array, so as to clearly distinguish this case, when the index is the MCID of a content item, from the case of a "non-existent" MCID (the previous bullet point).
>
> One possibility is to use for this case the structure tree root.

 [(comment 1717385006)](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/308#issuecomment-1717385006):
> The idea is that this is simply better than using "null" as the "distinguished value" for both cases. Like "null" it is really just a name, not an actual "structure parent".

[(comment 1717443543)](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/308#issuecomment-1717443543):
> no one is adding any children to the root, it is merely used as an arbitrary marker, that is not "null".
>
> If no one likes it then choose something else, such as "the integer 0".

IMO, this proposal has a lot of merit, for a purpose I will explain after a short preamble. As @car222222 [highlighted](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/308#issuecomment-1626680008)...
> The MCID numbers of the content items in a content stream can be arbitrary integers, they need not form a 'complete integer interval' such as {0,1,2,3,4,5}; they can be any set, such as {0,2,4}, or even (in theory) {0,2,4,652}.

...and was [confirmed](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/308#issuecomment-1626379174) by the empirical evidence of @petervwyatt:
> I just ran a test over about 100,000 PDFs and a LOT of PDFs have this idiom with null in the array form of StructTreeRoot/ParentTree number-tree values (some with 100s and 1000s of instances)! [...]
>
> I did not check the content streams and whether any MCID still indexed those null array elements.

I ran into such cases myself (not a big set though, so nothing statistically significant), finding with horror `StructTreeRoot`/`ParentTree` array values with a tiny bunch of indirect references preceded by over 8,000 `null` elements:
`[ `... over 8,000 null ...` null null null 4935 0 R 4935 0 R 4935 0 R 4935 0 R 4935 0 R 4936 0 R 4936 0 R 4936 0 R 4936 0 R 4936 0 R 4936 0 R 4936 0 R 4937 0 R 4937 0 R 4937 0 R 4937 0 R 4937 0 R 4938 0 R 4938 0 R 4938 0 R 4938 0 R 4938 0 R 4938 0 R 4938 0 R 4939 0 R 4939 0 R 4939 0 R 4939 0 R 4939 0 R 4939 0 R 4939 0 R 4939 0 R 4939 0 R 4939 0 R 4939 0 R 4939 0 R 4939 0 R 4939 0 R 4940 0 R ]`

I did my check on those content streams and found no marked-content sequence other than those actually indexed in their `StructTreeRoot`/`ParentTree` array values. So in my case [it was presumably a deliberated denormalization](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/308#issuecomment-1721239796) (ie, a violation of the recommendation in NOTE of 14.7.5.4 (Finding structure elements from content items): "Because marked-content identifiers serve as indices into an array in the structural parent tree, their assigned values need to be as small as possible to conserve space in the array.") — I wouldn't be surprised if a sizable part of @petervwyatt's PDFs fell under this abominable case.

Deliberated denormalizations aside, `StructTreeRoot`/`ParentTree` array values are prone to entropic decay by their very own nature: they were clearly conceived to pack a tight bunch of references in the smallest space possible, on the assumption of careful processing to prevent them from falling apart; hence, *beside missing to state the use of `null` array elements (**file format requirement**)*, IMHO, *ISO PDF fails also to explicitly state* (other than the timid NOTE in 14.7.5.4 (Finding structure elements from content items)) *the processing constraints (**processor requirement**) which should be honored by implementers to keep things in good shape*.

My proposal is to clearly state the **algorithm behind MCID assignment** in subclause 14.7.5.2 (Marked-content sequences as content items):
> When a marked-content sequence is assigned an MCID, it shall be the lowest available. For its determination, the processor scans the parent tree array associated to the content stream in which the sequence resides, looking for a free index (that is, a `*` element); if none is found, the next index shall be used (for example, if a 7-element array has no `*` element, the next index is 7, as the existing range is 0-6, inclusive). When an assigned MCID becomes unused (either because its marked-content sequence is deleted from the content stream or its entry in the property list of the marked-content sequence is removed), the corresponding element in the parent tree array shall be set to `*`; if it is the last element, the array shall be shrunk instead.

(where `*` is a distinctive value, as suggested by @car222222)

This algorithm deterministically prescibes which MCID shall be used in each and every case, ensuring the most compact `StructTreeRoot`/`ParentTree` array values possible without remapping the existing MCIDs. *The assumption here is that the indexes left free by ~deleted~/nonexistent/unused content items* (@car222222's point) *can be told apart from the indexes of orphaned content items* (@bdoubrov's point), so the proposal by @car222222 to mark orphaned content items with a distinctive value is definitely crucial for the purpose.

NOTE: *Because of backward compatibility, **`null` elements must be assumed as associated to orphaned content items*** (otherwise, editing legacy PDFs, MCIDs of orphaned content items could be inadvertently assigned to new marked-content sequences, ending up with duplicated MCIDs!). As a consequence, **it's array elements of ~deleted~/nonexistent/unused content items to have a distinctive value to be assigned to**, while orphaned content items must be assigned `null` value — this is the opposite of @car222222 proposal, but I'm confident he will be merciful ;)

DEFINITIONS

This comment uses terms previously adopted within this thread:
- **orphaned** means an MCID whose associated marked-content sequence reference was detached from the structure tree (that is, either the reference or any of its ancestor structure elements in the structure tree was removed from the `K` entry of the corresponding parent structure node (either structure element or structure root))
- **nonexistent/unused** means an MCID which is not associated to any marked-content sequence in the content stream (possibly because it was removed from its marked-content sequence or the marked-content sequence was deleted altogether)

IMPLEMENTATION NOTE

Implementers could be recommended to make available **maintenance procedures to normalize legacy PDFs**:
- basic maintenance: analyze marked-content sequences in content streams and update the elements of `StructTreeRoot`/`ParentTree` arrays with the distinctive value for ~deleted~/nonexistent/unused content items. For example, if the original structure is:
`[ null null 3743 0 R null null 3487 0 R null null null ]`
the normalized one would be (supposing `*` as distinctive value for ~deleted~/nonexistent/unused content items):
`[ * * 3743 0 R null * 3487 0 R * * null ]`
(remaining `null` elements represent actual orphaned content items)
- advanced maintenance: remap marked-content sequences in content streams with tight zero-based sequences of MCIDs and update the `StructTreeRoot`/`ParentTree` arrays accordingly. For example, the normalized structure of the original one (see example above) would be:
`[ 3743 0 R null 3487 0 R null ]`
(array elements indexed to ~deleted~/nonexistent/unused content items are purged)

> I would like to endorse @car222222's proposal about the **distinction between parent tree array elements for deleted/non-existing and orphaned content items**

I'm not quite sure what you are suggesting. I do understand the benefit in renumbering the MCID to get rid of unused 8000 `null`  entries, but what would be the benefit for a intermediate syntax like `[ * * 3743 0 R null * 3487 0 R * * null ]` from your basic maintainance? The purpose of the number tree is `Finding structure elements from content items`, that means a processor starts from a MCID in the stream goes to the array and looks up an index. It doesn't gain anything if unused index points are marked by * as it doesn't see them anyway doesn't it? It would still by 8000 index points it has to count.

Also it is imho unclear in the following sentences what you mean by "delete": Deleted from the content stream or deleted from the Kid array in the structure element? 

> When a marked-content sequence is deleted, the corresponding element in the parent tree array is set to null.

> (... supposing * as distinctive value for deleted/non-existing content items)

I think that the more common case is that when a structure element itself gets deleted.

It would have been a good idea if both this and the deletion of an MCS from the Kids array caused that MCS to lose its MCID entry.
Then there would not ever be any such MCS, that have an MCID and a Property list, but are not (despite their appearance) "content items". 

The question we therefore have is whether to distinguish between these cases:

An integer that has never appeared as an MCID in a PL of an MCS;

One that has so appeared but is now not the MCID of an MCS;

One that still appears as an MCID but only of an MCS that is not, in fact, a "content item".

The last case may not be theoretically possible  (depending on the, non-existent, precise definition of when an MCS is a "content item"); but in practice it is a very common case.
@stechio +1 for the phrase "deliberated denormalization" 🤹‍♂️

It is interesting that nothing explicitly states even that, in setting up an MCS as a "potential content item", the MCID assigned must be "unused" (whatever "unused" means!).  

For example, is it anywhere stated that it is either illegal or unwise, to reuse the MCID number of an orphaned MCS?

It doesn't gain anything if unused index points are marked by * as it doesn't see them anyway doesn't it? It would still by 8000 index points it has to count.

I considered the case of a processor **adding new marked-content sequences as content items to existing pages**: *since legacy PDFs mark parent tree array elements as `null` when indexed by either unused or orphaned MCIDs, there is no way to distinguish an unused index that is free to be assigned to a new content item*. The distinctive value (as proposed by @car222222) could be leveraged to identify such free index without wastefully inspecting the existing content stream or appending additional elements to its parent tree array. Of course, the advanced maintenance returns the normalized parent tree arrays without unused MCIDs, but maybe that's not always desirable/needed (for example, there may be a negligible number of `null` elements, so a remap affecting the entire content stream would be a waste of computational resources). *In any case, if editing a PDF results in new unused MCIDs, their parent tree array elements should be marked with the distinctive value* (say, `*`) *in order to make them distinguishable for reuse*, as explained here above.

> 
> > When a marked-content sequence is deleted, the corresponding element in the parent tree array is set to null.

I tried to adopt the same convention already in use in this thread, so:
- **orphaned** means an MCID whose associated marked-content sequence reference was detached from the structure tree (that is, either the reference or any of its ancestor structure elements in the structure tree was removed from the K entry of the corresponding parent structure node (either structure element or structure root))
- **unused/nonexistent** (formerly dubbed "deleted") means an MCID which is not associated to any marked-content sequence in the content stream (possibly because it was removed from its marked-content sequence or the marked-content sequence was deleted altogether)

> For example, is it anywhere stated that it is either illegal or unwise, to reuse the MCID number of an orphaned MCS?

If the processor finds a number MCID 42 in the stream and goes to the number tree, there is either a structure or `null` at index 42. So if you reuse the number the MCIDs are either both in the structure or both orphaned.  Inside the Kid array of the structure the 42 is referenced and the processor will probably roll a dice to which MCID in the stream this refers.

> I considered the case of a processor **adding new marked-content sequences as content items to existing pages**:

Ah, yes. That could be an use case.

> * **orphaned** means deleted from the `K` entry of the parent structure element
> * **unused/nonexistent** (formerly dubbed "deleted") means an MCID which is not associated to any marked-content sequence in the content stream (possibly because it was deleted from its marked-content sequence or the marked-content sequence was deleted altogether)

> When a marked-content sequence is deleted, the corresponding element in the parent tree array is set to null.

should be changed to

My question was not about how a processor may or may not react to this situation, rather about the existence of any documentation on the subject (or even a complete and watertight definition of a "content item".

@car222222: > @stechio +1 for the phrase "deliberated denormalization" 🤹‍♂️ Jokes aside, it's beyond my imagination that a processor could be forced by its users to torture tiny bunches of innocent marked-content sequences in hundreds of pages, ruthlessly deleting and regenerating them hundreds of times with ever-increasing MCIDs, so they would drift progressively and inescapably towards the infinite, like a cosmological inflation... It is statistically implausible that a streak of meaningful processing sessions could result in an isolated cluster of MCIDs on each of those pages — I would expect some non-null element scattered in-between, instead of a continuous sequence of thousands of `null` elements. *My educated guess is that the processor used **a global MCID counter for the whole PDF file*** (ouch!). Columns
  • Page index: zero-based page index (NOTE: additional occurrences represent nested content streams, ie form XObjects painted inside current page)
  • Indirect reference: content stream reference (either page or form XObject)
  • Parent tree array size: all the elements in the parent tree array associated to content stream

My feeling is that trading indexes (efficiency) for keys (flexibility) would be a lazy game without significant benefits and with certain drawbacks. In real-world applications, how would a dictionary of structural parents behave over time (editing session after editing session) compared to a (canonically generated and managed) array? Sure, the array could fragment with discarded MCIDs, or possibly expand when all discarded MCIDs are reused (as enforced by my algorithm proposal); the dictionary could shrink and expand, but its memory footprint would be often larger both in serialized and deserialized forms than its counterpart. Dictionaries would be somewhat more comfortable to juggle, but where is the solid gain of them as structural parents instead of current arrays? IMO, only a benchmark over a statistically-significant collection of real-world PDFs could clarify this point.

To add to @stechio's point, we generally try to avoid unconstrained dictionaries in PDF (even though in reality we do have a few, such as the role map dictionary).  Historically, this was to reserve the key names as "atoms" in a popular implementation, but since dictionaries have no order, walking them to find an entry would be inefficient.  Arrays seem like the right structure.

I agree with the outcome above, which is that only **StructParents** can have nulls and I don't think we can kill this off.  We also can't really mandate processor behaviors in generating these, since we're trying to just tell them how to build syntax.  A note added to the section on **StructParents** explaining that they can have null entries, but that it has negative impacts if used broadly (e.g. global MCID counters as mentioned previously) would be the right way forward.
Agreed that one would not want, in general, to use large dictionaries (for such purposes) unless they are implemented as hashed arrays so that look-up remains efficient.

Both sample files analyzed in this thread ([this](https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/26261VNR_Report_Finland_2020.pdf) for [Case 1](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/308#issuecomment-1721239796) and [this](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/files/12678388/cgc-principles-and-recommendations-fourth-edn.pdf) for [Case 2](https://github.com/pdf-association/pdf-issues/issues/308#issuecomment-1730439353)) were apparently produced by Adobe PDF Library (version 15.0), so *in these cases the **global MCID counter** cannot be a whimsical choice dictated by laziness*.

Trying to figure out a rationale behind that, page 39 of Case 2 seems to give a possible clue: *marked-content sequences nested in form XObjects* (see EXAMPLE 5 in subclause 14.7.5.2 (Marked-content sequences as content items)). Since form XObjects are inherently reusable, one might think that the MCIDs assigned to them couldn't be assigned elsewhere in the same file because of possible collisions. But subclause 14.7.5.4 (Finding structure elements from content items) clearly states that *each content stream (page object or other kind) has its own set of zero-based MCIDs* (emphasis is mine):
> For a content stream containing marked-content sequences that are content items, the value shall be an array of indirect references to the sequences' parent structure elements. The array element corresponding to each sequence shall be found by using the *sequence's marked-content identifier as a zero-based index into the array*.
> [...]
> Because a marked-content sequence is not an object in its own right, its parent tree key shall be found in the *StructParents entry of the page object or other content stream in which the sequence resides*. The value retrieved from the parent tree shall not be a reference to the parent structure element itself but to *an array of such references — one for each marked-content sequence contained within that content stream*.

So: an MCID is a ZERO-based index into an array of references to parent structure elements, ONE FOR EACH marked-content sequence contained WITHIN THAT content stream. Because of such definition, no collision is possible, isn't it? In turn, *the only plausible reason for global MCID counter vanishes miserably... (that wouldn't be decisive, anyway, since the overwhelming majority of `null` elements existing in those files are unrelated to form XObjects)*

**As Adobe PDF Library is, de facto, the gold standard among the implementations of ISO PDF, it would be great if @mrbhardy could let us reach out to its dev team to understand the rationale of their solution.**
